- 15-29: Tangential mentions — a business, policy, or science story that touches forestry/agriculture/mining in passing, or Cariboo civic news unrelated to working lands.

items.title: [space.com] Researchers grow potatoes in simulated lunar soil using 30% compost
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

Oregon State University researchers grew potatoes through their full life cycle in simulated lunar regolith after adding organic matter; a mixture containing 30% vermicompost produced yields comparable to those in terrestrial soil. The NASA-funded experiment took place in a greenhouse on Earth and used simulated material, not material collected on the moon, so it does not establish that crops can be grown on the lunar surface. The trial used five regolith simulants and the Modoc potato variety. Researchers plan to test 10 more potato varieties and are studying growth in larger pots; the first trial’s small pots produced small tubers.

items.title: [cbc.ca] Alberta bill sets data-centre limits and well cleanup funds
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

Alberta introduced Bill 42 on Nov. 18, proposing new siting and water rules for large data centres and mandatory cleanup funding for every new oil and gas well. Centres using at least 10 megawatts would generally have to be at least 600 metres from homes and avoid top-quality or irrigated farmland; they would also face a near-zero cooling-water standard. The Alberta Utilities Commission would regulate the larger facilities. The province says about 30% of current proposals could be affected, while projects already far along in approvals or construction would be exempt. For new wells, companies would pay up to $50,000 initially and make equal annual payments for up to 10 years. The money would remain attached to the well if ownership changes. If a well becomes orphaned, its funding would go to the Orphan Well Association. The requirements are expected to cover wells drilled after April 1, 2027. The bill would also eliminate Alberta’s oil-sands emissions cap, which the province says is redundant with industrial carbon pricing.

items.title: [leparisien.fr] Powerful El Niño nears December peak as droughts, fires threaten crops
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

The World Meteorological Organization says the powerful El Niño underway in the tropical Pacific is expected to peak in December and likely persist through February 2027, disrupting rainfall and raising drought and flood risks worldwide. Sea-surface temperatures in the key Niño 3.4 region rose from 1.6°C above normal in June to 2.5°C above normal in August; forecasters project temperatures about 3.7°C above normal in October-December, exceeding the previous record of 2.6°C above normal. Recent impacts include drought and fires in Brazil, extensive forest fires in Indonesia, and a possible 21% to 25% decline in Ivory Coast cocoa output. Researchers attributed Indonesia’s July-October rainfall deficit largely to El Niño, while saying human-caused climate change made the atmospheric conditions about three times more likely and more intense. The United Nations Development Programme says acting now to limit the impacts would cost $36 billion, compared with $73 billion if action is delayed.

items.title: [agri-mutuel.com] French institute plans AI farm adviser as Deere expands data tool
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

France’s public agricultural research institute INRAE plans to build an AI assistant using verified scientific data to help farmers respond to climate change and other pressures. The project awaits approval for €1.2 million in France 2030 funding, with a first version planned for farmer testing within 18 months. Separately, John Deere expanded access to its free JD assistant on Nov. 16, linking it to the company’s Operations Center farm-management platform. INRAE’s proposed assistant would tailor guidance to a farm’s location, practices, soil, expected water resources and finances, while Deere’s tool searches and analyzes information already recorded about a user’s fields, machinery and farm operations. INRAE says the project has demonstrated answers to simple queries and aims to handle more complex questions; farmer testing depends on the funding decision.

items.title: [thenationalnews.com] Black Sea attacks threaten grain routes as shipping costs rise
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

The United Nations warned that drone attacks on commercial vessels are threatening food exports as the Russia-Ukraine war spreads across shipping lanes. From June through October, the U.N. human rights office recorded reports of 164 attacks on commercial vessels around Ukraine’s Odesa and Mykolaiv regions and in the Black Sea; it verified 15 attacks that killed at least 21 vessel workers and injured 43. Recent strikes have also reached the Baltic and waters off Libya, while a maritime risk zone was extended on Nov. 18 toward Romania and Bulgaria. The disruption is raising freight and insurance costs and shifting grain purchases toward European suppliers, but prices are moving unevenly: Euronext’s December wheat contract closed Nov. 23 at €240.25 a tonne, up €3.50, while Constanța bread-wheat and corn quotes fell 1.7% and 1.3%. More Argentine and Australian wheat could become available to buyers in coming weeks.

items.content_html:

The International Energy Agency says the energy disruption linked to the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran is accelerating countries’ shift toward electrification. The agency said 25 countries had announced new electrification-related policies since February as governments seek more domestic energy sources. At the U.N. climate talks, COP31, host Türkiye is pressing to raise electricity’s share of global energy use from about 21% to 35% by 2035; draft negotiating text does not specify that the added power must come from renewables. The IEA also said buildings now use more energy for cooling than for heating, a shift it links to rising temperatures and demand for air conditioning. The agency expects solar and nuclear power to gain ground, but energy-security concerns could keep coal in use as backup, particularly in coal-rich Asian economies. It warned that inadequate electricity grids, charging infrastructure and supply capacity could slow electrification.

The Michigan Supreme Court declined to hear a challenge by dozens of townships to Public Act 233, the 2023 law that lets the state approve certain renewable energy projects when local zoning rules exceed the law’s standards. The justices have not resolved a separate dispute over when a 30-day deadline begins for local officials to tell developers they have a qualifying ordinance. They scheduled arguments for the January 2027 session and directed the parties to file briefs in December and January. The order does not approve or reject any specific energy project.

items.title: [krdo.com] Investigators suspect AI tool in breach of three US spy agencies
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

U.S. investigators suspect hackers used Artex, an AI-enabled penetration-testing framework, to breach an unclassified intelligence-analysis system used by the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA), the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI) and the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency (NGA). Early indicators point to China, but no attacker has been publicly identified. The network processes open-source intelligence, and officials have said classified information was not compromised. The network combines publicly available material with commercially sourced datasets, social-media content and satellite imagery. Investigators have not specified what records were accessed or when the breach occurred. An ODNI official said critical capabilities and classified systems were not disrupted, and a person familiar with the incident told The Associated Press the issue had been resolved. Separately, the Treasury Department’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) disclosed that it was investigating unauthorized access to a limited subset of its systems. The agency took some systems offline as a precaution, directed banks to use its Financial Institutions Hotline for reports, and said the FBI, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) and outside forensic examiners were assessing the incident.

items.title: [cybersecuritynews.com] Swiss agency confirms four successful AI-agent hacks, including attacks on critical-infrastructure operators
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

Switzerland’s National Cyber Security Centre says attackers using AI agents breached systems in four of five cases reported in the country, including attacks on three critical-infrastructure operators. The cases are part of a rise in campaigns using AI frameworks to automate reconnaissance and exploit security weaknesses. The Swiss agency has not identified the attackers, and officials reported no major outages. Italy’s incident response team says it observed campaigns in which multiple agents worked in parallel to compromise exposed systems. Canada’s cyber centre says automated tools have shortened some reconnaissance and exploitation from days or weeks to minutes. Amazon separately described agents that found and exploited an unpatched flaw on a university server in about 11 minutes. Swiss authorities advise organizations to reduce the number of internet-facing systems and install critical updates within 24 hours of release. Italy also urged operators to restrict remote-management access and monitor unusual authentication and network activity.

items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

The second beta of the smart home software Home Assistant 2026.12 makes it possible for the first time to connect cameras via the HomeKit Bridge and save their recordings with HomeKit Secure Video in Apple Home. Until now, the Bridge only transmitted live video; additional software was needed for recordings. Requirements include an Apple home hub, an iCloud+ subscription, a motion sensor, and setting up the camera as a standalone HomeKit accessory. Recording must be enabled separately for each camera. Recordings only start when motion is detected. As a result, the first few seconds may be missing. Home Assistant recommends H.264 streams, since conversion via FFmpeg uses processing power. In the developer test, an H.265 source failed to meet the Apple home hub’s time limit. The final version is planned for December 2, 2026; until then, beta features may still change.
